```{r}
#| label: setup
#| eval: false
library(DeCovarT)
```

The [bivariate toy](R1-bivariate-toy.html) fits the population
convolution, whose bulk covariance is $\sum_jp_j^2\boldsymbol\Sigma_j$.
The model that DeCovarT fits on real bulks is the single-cell model: a
bulk is the sum of $n_i$ cells, and its covariance is linear in the
composition
([single-cell model](02-1-single-cell-generative-optimisation.html)).
This scenario rebuilds the toy on that model, with the same two genes,
the same two cell types and the same small centroid gap. Three things
vary: the composition, the number of cells per bulk and the two
gene–gene correlations. The aim is to compare the optimisers
(Newton–Raphson, L-BFGS-B, Marquardt–Levenberg) and the interval
constructions on a likelihood that can be drawn in full. Construction,
benchmark and figures live in one script,
`scripts/fig05_bivariate_single_cell.R` (seed `20261125`).

# Generative model {#sec-scb-generative}

Bulk $i$ draws its cell counts, then the exact Gaussian sum of those
cells (`simulate_bulk_from_cells()`, platform scale $a=1$):

$$
\boldsymbol m_{\cdot i}\sim\operatorname{Multinomial}(n_i,\boldsymbol p^{\star}),
\qquad
\boldsymbol y_{\cdot i}\mid\boldsymbol m_{\cdot i}
\sim\mathcal N_2\bigl(n_i\tilde{\boldsymbol\mu}\boldsymbol p_{\cdot i},\;
n_i\boldsymbol S_W(\boldsymbol p_{\cdot i})\bigr),
\qquad
\boldsymbol p_{\cdot i}=\boldsymbol m_{\cdot i}/n_i,
$$ {#eq-scb-generator}

with $\boldsymbol S_W(\boldsymbol p)=\sum_jp_j\boldsymbol\Sigma_{W,j}$. The
mean scale $c_i=a\,n_i$ and the variance scale $\phi_i=a^2n_i$ both
equal $n_i$. The estimand is the **realised** fraction
$\boldsymbol p_{\cdot i}$, as in the
[two-lineage scenario](R4-single-cell-hierarchical.html#sec-sc-generative).

- The per-cell means are $\tilde{\boldsymbol\mu}_{\cdot1}=(20,22)$ and
  $\tilde{\boldsymbol\mu}_{\cdot2}=(22,20)$ counts per cell: the small
  centroid gap of the population toy.
- The per-cell covariances are
  $\boldsymbol\Sigma_{W,j}=500\,\boldsymbol R_j$, with $\boldsymbol R_j$
  the exchangeable correlation matrix of $\varrho_j$. A per-cell variance
  of 500 at a mean of about 21 counts is a coefficient of variation of
  1.06, the variance of a negative binomial with dispersion
  $\theta\approx0.92$.
- The number of cells per bulk is drawn around a nominal value
  $n\in\{10^2,10^3,10^4\}$: each bulk draws
  $n_i=\operatorname{round}\{n\exp(\sigma z-\sigma^2/2)\}$,
  $z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$, $\sigma^2=\log(1+0.3^2)$: a log-normal count of
  mean $n$ and coefficient of variation $30\%$.

Per cell, $\boldsymbol y_{\cdot i}/n_i$ has covariance
$\boldsymbol S_W(\boldsymbol p)/n_i$. At $n=1000$ and
$\boldsymbol p=(1/2,1/2)$ it equals the homoscedastic bulk covariance
$\tfrac14(\boldsymbol R_1+\boldsymbol R_2)$ of the population toy
(<!-- chk: V49a -->ledger V49a), so that page of this scenario has the
same means, the same bulk covariance and the same Fisher information as
the corresponding page of §2.2. The two models part at other
compositions: at $\boldsymbol p=(0.99,0.01)$ the population covariance is
close to $\boldsymbol R_1$, the single-cell one to $\tfrac12\boldsymbol R_1$,
because the weights are $p_j^2$ in one and $p_j$ in the other. The
number of cells moves the bulk variance by a factor of ten each way,
from about five times to a twentieth of the population toy's.

## Why the scales are given

With $G=2$ genes, one bulk cannot identify $c_i$ or $\phi_i$. The mean
$c\,\tilde{\boldsymbol\mu}\boldsymbol p$ has two free parameters, $c$ and
$p_1$, for two observations, so it fits any bulk inside the cone of the
two signatures exactly. The residual is then zero, the closed-form
$\hat\phi=\boldsymbol r^\top\boldsymbol W\boldsymbol r/G$ is zero, and the
profiled log-likelihood has no maximum. The REML degrees of freedom are
$\nu=G-J=0$. Every scale-dependent fit therefore receives $c_i$ and
$\phi_i$ (`mean_scale`, `variance_scale`), and only $p_1$ is estimated.
`deconvolute_single_cell()` accepts $G=J$ only on that path.

In practice $n_i$ is not known. Each such method therefore runs twice.
The oracle arm receives the true $n_i$ of the bulk, the best case. The
nominal arm receives the design value $n$, the realistic case, whose
error has a coefficient of variation of 30%. A wrong $c$ moves
$\boldsymbol y/c$ along $\tilde{\boldsymbol\mu}\boldsymbol p^\star$,
which is orthogonal to the segment between the two signatures only for
the balanced composition, and a wrong $\phi$ rescales the covariance.

## Information in the mean and in the covariance

At known scales, the Fisher information of $p_1$ at $\boldsymbol p^\star$
splits into a mean part and a covariance part
(<!-- chk: V49c -->ledger V49c):

$$
I(p_1)=n\,\boldsymbol d^\top\boldsymbol S_W(\boldsymbol p^\star)^{-1}\boldsymbol d
+\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}\bigl[\{\boldsymbol S_W(\boldsymbol p^\star)^{-1}
(\boldsymbol\Sigma_{W,1}-\boldsymbol\Sigma_{W,2})\}^2\bigr],
\qquad
\boldsymbol d=\tilde{\boldsymbol\mu}_{\cdot1}-\tilde{\boldsymbol\mu}_{\cdot2}.
$$ {#eq-scb-fisher}

The mean part grows with $n$; the covariance part does not, and it is
zero when $\varrho_1=\varrho_2$. Its share
$f_{\mathrm{cov}}=I_{\mathrm{cov}}/I$ is recorded for every scenario
(`fisher_mean`, `fisher_cov`, `f_cov` in the config).

| Composition | $n$ | median $f_{\mathrm{cov}}$ | $f_{\mathrm{cov}}$ at $(\varrho_1,\varrho_2)=(-0.8,0.8)$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| balanced | 100 | 0.20 | 0.62 |
| balanced | 1,000 | 0.024 | 0.14 |
| balanced | 10,000 | 0.0024 | 0.016 |
| moderately unbalanced | 100 | 0.20 | 0.87 |
| moderately unbalanced | 1,000 | 0.025 | 0.41 |
| moderately unbalanced | 10,000 | 0.0025 | 0.065 |
| highly unbalanced | 100 | 0.20 | 0.97 |
| highly unbalanced | 1,000 | 0.024 | 0.76 |
| highly unbalanced | 10,000 | 0.0025 | 0.24 |

: Share of the Fisher information of $p_1$ carried by the covariances, over the 81 correlation pairs of each page (median) and at the opposite-sign corner. {#tbl-scb-fcov}

With uncorrelated genes the information is $0.016\,n$ in every
composition: a standard error of $p_1$ of $0.79$ at $n=100$, $0.25$ at
$n=1000$ and $0.079$ at $n=10^4$. At $n=100$ the means alone barely
locate $p_1$ in $(0,1)$; opposite correlations then carry most of what
can be learnt.

## Factorial design

| Factor | Levels |
|---|---|
| Composition $\boldsymbol p^\star$ | balanced $(1/2,1/2)$; moderately unbalanced $(17/20,3/20)$; highly unbalanced $(99/100,1/100)$ |
| Cells per bulk $n$ (nominal) | $10^2$; $10^3$; $10^4$ |
| Gene–gene corr. CT 1 ($\varrho_1$) | $\{-0.8,-0.6,\ldots,0.8\}$, 9 levels |
| Gene–gene corr. CT 2 ($\varrho_2$) | $\{-0.8,-0.6,\ldots,0.8\}$, 9 levels |
| Fixed | means $(20,22)$, $(22,20)$; $\boldsymbol\Sigma_{W,j}=500\,\boldsymbol R_j$; $a=1$; equal cell sizes |
| **Total scenarios** | $3\times3\times9\times9=\mathbf{729}$ |

: Bivariate single-cell factorial. {#tbl-scb-factorial}

Scenario identifiers read `SB{index}_{Ba|Mo|Hi}_n{1e2|1e3|1e4}`, for
example `SB122_Ba_n1e3` ($\varrho_1=\varrho_2=0$, balanced, $n=1000$).
The heteroscedastic and large-gap levels of §2.2 are not crossed here:
the cell count already moves the bulk variance, and $n_i$ cannot create
the gene-specific variance ratio of the heteroscedastic level.

With the highly unbalanced composition and $n=100$, the rare type counts
one cell on average, and $37\%$ of the bulks hold none: their target
sits on a face of the simplex. Wald and ILR intervals are undefined
there, so their coverage is over interior targets; the
[boundary test](#sec-scb-boundary) uses exactly these bulks.

```{r}
#| label: design
source("scripts/fig05_bivariate_single_cell.R")
config <- build_bivariate_single_cell_config()
nrow(config)
dplyr::count(config, proportions, n_cells)
```

# Inference {#sec-scb-inference}

Every method is scored on the same simulated bulks.

| Method | Function or code | Input | Intervals |
|:-------|:-----------------|:------|:----------|
| `lsei` | `deconvolute_ratios_deconrnaseq()` on $\boldsymbol y/c$ | true means, plug-in $c$ | none |
| NNLS | `deconvolute_ratios_nnls()` | true means (free scale) | none |
| Newton–Raphson | `deconvolute_single_cell(optimiser = "newton")` | true moments, plug-in scales | Wald, ILR, profile, oracle; bootstrap (8 scenarios) |
| L-BFGS-B | `deconvolute_single_cell(optimiser = "lbfgsb")` | true moments, plug-in scales | Wald, ILR |
| Marquardt–Levenberg | `deconvolute_single_cell(optimiser = "marquardt")` | true moments, plug-in scales | Wald, ILR |
| Firth | `fit_firth_single_cell()` | true moments, plug-in scales | Wald, ILR |
| DeCovarT diagonal | Newton–Raphson with the off-diagonals of $\boldsymbol\Sigma_{W,j}$ set to zero | true variances, plug-in scales | Wald, ILR |
| RNA-Sieve | `rnasieve` 0.1.4 (Python), corrected update | reference panel, cohort of $N$ bulks | released, Fisher, Godambe |
| ReDeconv | `redeconv` 1.2.1 (Python) | true means and standard deviations | none |

: Methods of the bivariate single-cell benchmark. Every method with a plug-in runs in the oracle and the nominal arm. {#tbl-scb-methods}

- The three DeCovarT solvers maximise the same
  log-likelihood at the same plug-in scales. Newton–Raphson and
  Marquardt–Levenberg work in the ILR coordinate; Newton uses the PORT
  trust region of `stats::nlminb()`, Marquardt–Levenberg adds Levenberg
  damping and stops on the relative distance to the maximum
  [@marquardtAlgorithmLeastSquaresEstimation1963;
  @commengesNewtonLikeAlgorithmLikelihood2006; @R-marqLevAlg]. L-BFGS-B
  runs on the closure chart $\boldsymbol p=\boldsymbol w/\mathbf1^\top\boldsymbol w$,
  $\boldsymbol w\ge0$, and can return exact zeros
  [@byrdLimitedMemoryAlgorithm1995]. Firth maximises the
  Jeffreys-penalised log-likelihood
  [@firthBiasReductionMaximum1993].
- DeCovarT diagonal fits the model of RNA-Sieve
  [@erdmann-phamLikelihoodbasedDeconvolutionBulk2021]: independent genes,
  a variance linear in the cell counts. Run at the true variances and
  scales, it isolates what the gene–gene correlation adds; its intervals
  are those of the diagonal (working) model. RNA-Sieve itself estimates
  the reference from a panel of $R$ individuals with 20 cells per type
  each (`simulate_reference_replicates()`, own seed) and fits the cohort
  of $N$ bulks jointly. The released `_minimize_alpha` passes its
  simplex constraints to `cp.Minimize()`; under cvxpy 1.6 that raises an
  error the package catches, and the proportions never leave their start.
  The runner replaces it with the corrected update
  (`scripts/benchmark_metrics/python/run_rnasieve.py`).
- `lsei` reads the bulk per cell $\boldsymbol y/c$
  with the plug-in $c$ and keeps $\mathbf1^\top\boldsymbol p=1$
  [@gongDeconRNASeqStatisticalFramework2013]; NNLS fits a free scale and
  renormalises [@dessoleLawsonHansonAlgorithmDeviation2023], so it needs
  no plug-in.
- Eight methods are not run. DWLS [@tsoucasAccurateEstimationCelltype2019] chooses its
  dampening constant on random halves of the genes; at $G=2$ a half is
  one gene, and `DWLS::solveDampenedWLS()` (0.1.0) stops on every bulk.
  RLM and CIBERSORT regress two observations on two signatures; MEAD
  and DECALS rely on asymptotics in the number of genes, and DECALS'
  point estimate is `lsei`. BayesPrism, SCDC and DeMixSC need count data
  or many genes.

## Interval constructions {#sec-scb-intervals}

| Interval | Construction | Methods |
|:---------|:-------------|:--------|
| `wald` | delta method on $p_1$, from the observed information at the plug-in scales | DeCovarT solvers, Firth |
| `ilr` | Wald in the ILR coordinate, mapped back to the simplex | DeCovarT solvers, Firth |
| `profile` | likelihood-ratio inversion at the plug-in scales (interior, $\chi^2_1$) | Newton–Raphson |
| `oracle` | $\hat p_1$ plus or minus the Wald half-width at the true composition | Newton–Raphson |
| `bootstrap` | percentile interval of $B=199$ parametric refits at the plug-in scales | Newton–Raphson, 8 scenarios |
| `bootstrap_nprior` | as `bootstrap`, with $n$ redrawn from its log-normal law in every replicate | Newton–Raphson, nominal arm, 8 scenarios |

: Interval menu ([population inference](01-2-population-inference.html#sec-recap)). {#tbl-scb-menu}

The bootstrap runs on the eight scenarios
$\{$balanced, moderately unbalanced$\}\times\{n=100,1000\}\times
\{(\varrho_1,\varrho_2)=(0,0),(-0.8,0.8)\}$. In the nominal arm the
other intervals treat $n$ as known, so they ignore its 30% error.
`bootstrap_nprior` draws each replicate at
$n\exp(\sigma z-\sigma^2/2)$ and refits at the nominal $n$: it carries
the uncertainty of the cell count into the interval
(`bootstrap_single_cell(n_cells_sdlog = )`).

A Godambe sandwich is not run: it needs independent score
contributions, and one bulk of two correlated genes has two dependent
ones. Coverage is reported with a Wilson Monte Carlo interval
[@morrisUsingSimulationStudies2019].

## Boundary test of an absent cell type {#sec-scb-boundary}

For every bulk, `lrt_single_cell(null_value = c(celltype_2 = 0))`
compares the fit with the vertex $\boldsymbol p=(1,0)$, at the oracle and
at the nominal scales. The null lies on a face, so the statistic is
referred to $\tfrac12\chi^2_0+\tfrac12\chi^2_1$
[@selfAsymptoticPropertiesMaximum1987]. Bulks that hold no type-2 cell
measure its size; the others its power.

## Run size

| Constant | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `N_REPLICATES` | Monte Carlo bulks per scenario, $N$ | 200 |
| `N_REFERENCE` | individuals of the reference panel, $R$ (RNA-Sieve) | 200 |
| `N_BOOT` | bootstrap replicates, $B$ | 199 |
| `CORES` | workers for the $N$ bulks of a scenario | a third of half the cores (14 of 88) |
| `RUN_DWLS` | run DWLS | `FALSE` (fails at $G=2$) |

: Run-size constants at the top of `scripts/fig05_bivariate_single_cell.R`; `FIG05_POSTPROCESS_ONLY=1` redraws the figures. {#tbl-scb-run-size}

# Results {#sec-scb-results}

Each figure stem is one multi-page PDF,
`output/fig05/{density,performance}_visualisations/<stem>.pdf`, with
the RDS of the data that drew it next to it (`<stem>.rds`). The RDS
holds the tables in long format and a `pages` table that names each
page (`page_id`, the page label and, for the interval forests, the
scenario `ID`). One page is redrawn from that RDS alone, as an SVG under
`<stem>/<page_id>.svg`:

```{r}
#| label: redraw
source("scripts/visualisation/load_visualisation.R")
book <- readRDS("output/fig05/performance_visualisations/heatmap_rmse.rds")
book$pages
render_figure_from_data("heatmap_rmse", book, "output/fig05", page = "balanced_n_1000")
```

| Stem | Description |
|---|---|
| `purified_density`, `bulk_density` | Laws per cell: bulks of one type, $\mathcal N(\tilde{\boldsymbol\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol\Sigma_{W,j}/n)$, and the bulk, $\mathcal N(\tilde{\boldsymbol\mu}\boldsymbol p,\boldsymbol S_W(\boldsymbol p)/n)$ |
| `loglik_surface_p`, `loglik_expected_surface_p` | Log-likelihood of one bulk, and its expectation, on $(p_1,p_2)$ at the true scales |
| `loglik_ilr_profile`, `loglik_expected_ilr_profile` | The same along the ILR coordinate |
| `loglik_mean_shift_slice`, `loglik_correlation_slice` | Expected log-likelihood of $p_1$ at fixed $\boldsymbol p^\star$ while the mean or the correlation of cell type 1 moves; Fisher information split as in @eq-scb-fisher |
| `heatmap_rmse`, `heatmap_aitchison` | Tiles on $(\varrho_1,\varrho_2)$, one row per arm |
| `rmse_colour_aitchison_size_dots` | Colour = mean RMSE, size = mean Aitchison distance |
| `ci_width_forest` | Mean interval, coverage [Wilson interval] and width, per corner scenario |
| `p_hat_monte_carlo_raincloud`, `p_hat_monte_carlo_quantile_dots` | Monte Carlo law of $\hat p_1$ |
| `wald_normality_qq`, `wald_mahalanobis_chi2_qq` | Whitened ILR estimate, information at the true scales |
| `estimate_agreement_hellinger_ward` | Mean Hellinger distance between paired estimates, Ward clustering |
| `kkt_residual_raincloud`, `convergence_theoretical_vs_numerical_failures` | Projected-score KKT residual; theoretical and numerical failures |
| `boundary_lrt` | Size and power of the boundary test of $p_2=0$ |
| `runtime`, `memory` | $\log_{10}$ seconds and MiB |

: Figure books of the bivariate single-cell scenario. There is no 3D surface. {#tbl-scb-books}

## Results description {#sec-scb-results-description}

The full run used $N=200$ bulks per scenario (commit `9014f90`, 25
November 2026, 12,769 s on 14 workers). No method failed numerically
on any bulk. Unless stated otherwise, a number below is the median over
the 81 correlation pairs of a page of the per-scenario root mean squared
error (RMSE) of $\hat p_1$, or the mean over those pairs of the
coverage of a nominal 95% interval. The values are printed by
`Rscript scripts/fig05_summary_numbers.R` from
`output/fig05/fig05_benchmark.rds`.

### Point estimates

| Composition | $n$ | `lsei` | Newton | Marquardt | Firth | Newton, nominal $n$ | `lsei`, nominal $n$ | NNLS | RNA-Sieve |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| balanced | 100 | 0.414 | 0.429 | 0.395 | 0.390 | 0.460 | 0.409 | 0.414 | 0.410 |
| balanced | 1,000 | 0.243 | 0.249 | 0.242 | 0.187 | 0.397 | 0.238 | 0.244 | 0.249 |
| balanced | 10,000 | 0.081 | 0.082 | 0.082 | 0.076 | 0.378 | 0.078 | 0.081 | 0.106 |
| moderately unbalanced | 100 | 0.424 | 0.445 | 0.423 | 0.419 | 0.435 | 0.422 | 0.424 | 0.432 |
| moderately unbalanced | 1,000 | 0.201 | 0.200 | 0.199 | 0.215 | 0.188 | 0.195 | 0.201 | 0.207 |
| moderately unbalanced | 10,000 | 0.080 | 0.080 | 0.080 | 0.079 | 0.142 | 0.107 | 0.080 | 0.103 |
| highly unbalanced | 100 | 0.457 | 0.455 | 0.436 | 0.453 | 0.459 | 0.456 | 0.458 | 0.447 |
| highly unbalanced | 1,000 | 0.179 | 0.182 | 0.182 | 0.236 | 0.199 | 0.191 | 0.179 | 0.179 |
| highly unbalanced | 10,000 | 0.061 | 0.061 | 0.061 | 0.093 | 0.099 | 0.105 | 0.061 | 0.047 |

: RMSE of $\hat p_1$, median over the 81 correlation pairs. Columns without "nominal $n$" use the true $n_i$ (oracle arm) or need no cell count (NNLS, RNA-Sieve). {#tbl-scb-rmse}

With the true $n_i$, the three DeCovarT solvers, `lsei`, NNLS and
DeCovarT diagonal are within 0.035 of each other on every page
(@tbl-scb-rmse). DeCovarT diagonal returns the `lsei` RMSE to within
0.002 everywhere; ReDeconv returns the NNLS RMSE to four. The
standard errors announced by @tbl-scb-fcov for uncorrelated genes
(0.79, 0.25 and 0.079 at $n=100$, 1,000 and $10^4$) set the scale: at
$n=100$ every method is close to a random guess on $(0,1)$, and at
$n=10^4$ every method is at or below that standard error.

Along the correlation grid, the full-covariance Newton fit differs from
`lsei` by at most 15% in median RMSE (@fig-scb-heatmap). Its RMSE ratio
to `lsei` rises with $|\varrho_1-\varrho_2|$ for the balanced
composition at $n=100$ (1.12 at $|\varrho_1-\varrho_2|=1.6$) and falls
with it for the highly unbalanced composition at $n=1000$ (0.85 at
1.6). Over the 243 scenarios of each $n$, Newton beats `lsei` by more
than 5% in 18%, 15% and 3% of them at $n=100$, 1,000 and $10^4$, and
loses by more than 5% in 36%, 10% and 0%.

![RMSE of $\hat p_1$ on the $(\varrho_1,\varrho_2)$ grid, balanced composition, $n=1000$. Top row: oracle arm; middle row: nominal arm; bottom row: methods without a plug-in. One $\log_{10}$ colour scale for every page of the book.](figures/fig05/performance_visualisations__heatmap_rmse__balanced_n_1000.svg){#fig-scb-heatmap fig-alt="Grid of 15 heatmaps, one per method and arm, with the correlation of cell type 1 on the x axis and of cell type 2 on the y axis. In the oracle row all methods show similar colours, RMSE near 0.2 to 0.3. In the nominal row Newton-Raphson, L-BFGS-B and Firth are lighter (higher RMSE) everywhere except on the diagonal where the two correlations are equal, while lsei and DeCovarT diagonal look like their oracle panels."}

The plug-in cell count matters more than the correlation. With the
nominal $n$, the Newton RMSE grows by a median factor of 1.06, 1.58 and
4.44 at $n=100$, 1,000 and $10^4$ for the balanced composition, and of
1.69 and 2.20 at $n=10^4$ for the highly and moderately unbalanced
ones (90th percentiles up to 8.2). The loss sits off the diagonal
$\varrho_1=\varrho_2$ (@fig-scb-heatmap, middle row): at
$(\varrho_1,\varrho_2)=(0,0)$ the balanced RMSE at $n=10^4$ is 0.081
with the true $n_i$ and 0.079 with the nominal $n$; at $(-0.8,0.8)$ it is
0.082 and 0.330. `lsei` and DeCovarT diagonal keep their oracle RMSE for
the balanced composition (ratio 0.96 to 0.99) but lose a factor of
about 1.4 (moderately unbalanced) and 1.6 to 1.8 (highly unbalanced)
at $n=10^4$.

### Solvers

With the true $n_i$, Newton–Raphson, L-BFGS-B and Marquardt–Levenberg
return the same $\hat p_1$ to within $10^{-5}$ in the median bulk at
every $n$. They part at $n=100$: $|\hat p_1^{\mathrm{NR}}-\hat
p_1^{\mathrm{ML}}|>0.01$ in 16% to 20% of the bulks and
$|\hat p_1^{\mathrm{NR}}-\hat p_1^{\mathrm{L\text{-}BFGS\text{-}B}}|>0.01$
in 6% to 10%. L-BFGS-B stops on a face of the simplex in 51% to 63% of
the bulks at $n=100$, and in 44% to 50% of the highly unbalanced bulks
at $n=1000$ and $10^4$. The two ILR solvers never return a face. The
log-likelihood of the truth exceeds that of the estimate by more than
$10^{-3}$ in 4.6%, 1.1% and 0.2% of the Newton fits at $n=100$, 1,000
and $10^4$ (Marquardt–Levenberg: 4.3%, 1.0%, 0.09%; L-BFGS-B: 0.2%,
0.006%, 0%). Median times per bulk are 2 ms (L-BFGS-B), 3 ms (Newton),
4 to 9 ms (Marquardt–Levenberg), 11 ms (Firth) and 130 ms (RNA-Sieve).

Firth's penalty lowers the balanced RMSE at $n=1000$ from 0.249 to 0.187
and raises the highly unbalanced one from 0.182 to 0.236, with a median
bias of $-0.16$ there.

With the true $n_i$, the profile interval covers at 0.95 to 0.99 on
every page (@tbl-scb-coverage). The Wald interval under-covers at
$n=100$ (0.76 to 0.83) and reaches 0.90 to 0.96 from $n=1000$. The ILR

its mean width is then 0.78 to 1.00; it covers 0.57 to 0.71 for the highly unbalanced composition.

The bootstrap sub-study separates the two correlation corners. At
$(0,0)$, every construction covers 0.94 to 1.00 in both arms, except
the nominal-arm Wald interval (0.88 balanced at $n=100$, 0.86
moderately unbalanced at $n=1000$). At $(-0.8,0.8)$ with the true
$n_i$, the Wald interval covers 0.44 to 0.85, the parametric bootstrap
0.79 to 0.92 and the profile interval 0.93 to 0.985. With the nominal
$n$ at $(-0.8,0.8)$, the mean Newton estimate for the balanced composition at
$n=1000$ moves from 0.46 to 0.19, against a mean target of 0.50, while
DeCovarT diagonal stays at 0.49 in both arms (@fig-scb-forest), and coverage falls to
0.05–0.25 (Wald), 0.28–0.69 (profile) and 0.38–0.79 (bootstrap).
Redrawing $n$ from its log-normal law in each bootstrap replicate
lowers coverage in all four of these scenarios, to 0.17–0.67.

### Boundary test

Of the 16,200 highly unbalanced bulks at $n=100$, 6,130 hold no type-2
cell. On them the boundary test rejects $p_2=0$ in 3.7% of the bulks
with the true $n_i$ and in 16.1% with the nominal $n$
(@fig-scb-boundary). When type 2 is present at $p_2=0.01$, the test
rejects in 4.4%, 5.5% and 6.9% of the bulks at $n=100$, 1,000 and
$10^4$ with the true $n_i$, close to the 5% level. Power reaches 0.64
at $p_2=0.15$ and 0.9994 at $p_2=0.5$, both at $n=10^4$. With the
nominal $n$, the rejection rate at $p_2=0.01$ rises to 0.15 to 0.25 and
the power at $p_2=0.5$, $n=10^4$ falls to 0.81.

Power rises with n for the balanced composition to 1 at n = 10,000 with the true n, less with the nominal n. For the highly unbalanced composition the oracle rate stays near 0.05 at all n while the nominal-n rate is 0.15 to 0.25. Size at n = 100 is about 0.04 with the true n and 0.16 with the nominal n."}

### Likelihood geometry

The expected log-likelihood keeps its maximiser at $p_1^\star$ along
both slices (@fig-scb-slice; ledger V49d). Moving the mean of type 1
onto that of type 2 removes the mean part of the information. With
$(\varrho_1,\varrho_2)=(0.8,-0.8)$ the covariance part, $2.56$ at every
$n$ for the balanced composition, then carries the curvature; with
$(0,0)$ it is zero and the surface flattens as $t\to1$.

Bottom: Fisher information of $p_1$ at $p_1^\star$ and its mean and covariance parts (@eq-scb-fisher), log scale.](figures/fig05/density_visualisations__loglik_mean_shift_slice__balanced.svg){#fig-scb-slice fig-alt="Two-row figure. Top: heat maps of relative expected log-likelihood over p1 and the mean-shift t, for n = 100, 1,000 and 10,000 and two correlation pairs; all panels are maximal along p1 = 0.5 and flatten as t grows or n falls. Bottom: Fisher information against t; the mean part falls to zero as t approaches 1, the covariance part is flat, near 5 for opposite correlations and near zero for uncorrelated genes, so the total follows the covariance part only when correlations differ."}

## Discussion and interpretation of relative deconvolution performance {#sec-scb-discussion}

### The covariance part of the information is hard to use from one bulk

@tbl-scb-fcov gives the covariances up to 97% of the Fisher information
at $n=100$, yet the full-covariance fit is no more accurate than `lsei`
there and is worse in 36% of the scenarios. We read this as a
consequence of the design (inference, not tested separately): each
estimate rests on one bulk, and the covariance part of
@eq-scb-fisher is the information that a single draw of two genes
carries about its own spread. The mean part averages $n$ cells and
grows with $n$; the covariance part does not, and a single draw is far
from the regime where the maximum likelihood estimator attains the
Fisher bound. The Wald interval, built from the observed curvature,
under-covers at $n=100$ (0.76 to 0.83) and at the opposite-sign corner
(0.44 to 0.85), while the profile interval, which does not rely on the
quadratic approximation, holds its level. The full-covariance fit gains
where the mean part is already informative and the covariance share is
still large: highly unbalanced, $n=1000$, where $f_{\mathrm{cov}}$
reaches 0.76 and Newton's RMSE is 15% below `lsei`'s at
$|\varrho_1-\varrho_2|=1.6$.

DeCovarT diagonal reproduces `lsei` by construction in this design.
Both cell types have per-cell variance 500 on both genes, so the
diagonal $\boldsymbol S_W(\boldsymbol p)$ is $500\,\boldsymbol I$ for
every $\boldsymbol p$, and its likelihood is least squares on
$\boldsymbol y/c$ under the sum-to-one constraint. The comparison with
the full model therefore isolates the gene–gene correlation, as
intended, but says nothing about gene-specific variances.

### The cell count, not the correlation, limits accuracy

A 30% error in $n_i$ costs more than the correlation gains, and the cost
grows with $n$. With the nominal $n$, the scaled bulk is
$\boldsymbol y/n=(n_i/n)\,\tilde{\boldsymbol\mu}\boldsymbol p^\star$
plus noise of standard deviation about $\sqrt{500/n}$ per gene: the
misfit along $\tilde{\boldsymbol\mu}\boldsymbol p^\star$ is about
$0.3\times21\approx6$ against a noise of 0.22 at $n=10^4$. How much of
that misfit reaches $\hat p_1$ depends on the geometry:

- `lsei` projects $\boldsymbol y/n$ onto the segment between the
  signatures in the Euclidean metric. For the balanced composition,
  $\tilde{\boldsymbol\mu}\boldsymbol p^\star=(21,21)$ is orthogonal to
  $\boldsymbol d=(-2,2)$ and the misfit leaves $\hat p_1$ unchanged; for
  the unbalanced compositions it is not orthogonal, which matches the
  loss by a factor of 1.4 to 1.8 at $n=10^4$.
- The full-covariance fit projects in the
  $\boldsymbol S_W(\boldsymbol p)^{-1}$ metric, and when
  $\varrho_1\ne\varrho_2$ its covariance depends on $\boldsymbol p$, so
  the fit also moves $\hat{\boldsymbol p}$ to match a spread that a
  wrong $\phi$ has rescaled. On the diagonal $\varrho_1=\varrho_2$,
  $\boldsymbol S_W$ does not depend on $\boldsymbol p$ and $(1,1)$ is one
  of its eigenvectors, so the balanced fit stays unbiased there: the
  darker diagonal of the nominal row of @fig-scb-heatmap.

None of the interval constructions repairs this, because the failure is
a bias of the point estimate, not an underestimated variance. Redrawing
$n$ in the bootstrap makes it worse: each replicate is refitted at the
nominal $n$ around an already biased $\hat p_1$, so its percentiles
probably carry the bias twice (not checked).

In practice $n_i$ is unknown, and at $G=2$ it cannot be estimated
(@sec-scb-generative). Two routes avoid the plug-in. A scale-free fit
(NNLS with a free scale, renormalised; ReDeconv returns the same
estimates here) matched the oracle `lsei` on every page without any
cell count. With $G>J$ genes, the scales enter the likelihood and can
be profiled ([§2.5](R4-single-cell-hierarchical.html)). The covariance-aware
fit at a plugged-in $n$ is worth its cost only when $n_i$ is measured,
for instance from nuclei counts.

### Choice of solver

The three DeCovarT solvers agree in the interior; they differ when the
maximum lies on, or near, a face. L-BFGS-B works on the closed simplex,
reaches the face and returns the highest log-likelihood most often
(truth above the estimate in at most 0.2% of bulks, against 4.6% for
Newton at $n=100$). The ILR solvers cannot reach a face, and they are
the ones whose Hessian feeds the Wald, ILR and profile intervals. A
practical sequence is L-BFGS-B for the point estimate and the face
diagnosis, then Newton–Raphson from that point for the intervals when
the estimate is interior; the benchmark did not run that sequence.
At $n=100$, Marquardt–Levenberg and Newton–Raphson differ by more than
0.01 in 16% to 20% of the bulks, and Marquardt–Levenberg has the lower
RMSE on all three compositions (by 0.02 to 0.03). Both stop where the
gradient vanishes, so the gap points to several local maxima, reached
from the same start by different step sequences.

Firth's penalty pulls $\hat p_1$ towards $1/2$: it lowers the balanced
RMSE by a quarter at $n=1000$ and biases the highly unbalanced estimate
by $-0.16$, with ILR coverage 0.04. It is not a safe default when a
cell type may be rare.

### Detecting a rare cell type

With the true $n_i$, the chi-bar-square boundary test keeps its size
(3.7% at the 5% level). With these signatures, two genes and a mean gap
of 2 counts per cell, it cannot detect a type at 1% even at $n=10^4$.
With the nominal $n$, it rejects $p_2=0$ in 16% of the bulks that hold
no type-2 cell, so a wrong cell count turns into false detections.

### RNA-Sieve

RNA-Sieve, with the corrected update, matched DeCovarT within 0.025 in
RMSE on every page; it was better for the highly unbalanced composition
at $n=10^4$ (0.047 against 0.061) and worse for the balanced one (0.106
against 0.081). It fits the cohort of $N$ bulks jointly and estimates
the reference from the panel; which of the two drives these gaps is not
separated here. Its Fisher interval spans $[0,1]$ and carries no
information; its Godambe interval under-covers at $n=100$ (0.66 to
0.80).

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Caveats {#sec-scb-caveats}

- A sum of Gaussian cells is Gaussian at any $n_i$,
  and 17% of the per-cell values (the reference panel of RNA-Sieve) are
  negative; a count layer
  would be needed to test the central-limit step itself.
- Every DeCovarT fit reads the true moments; the
  reference panel enters only through RNA-Sieve.
- Each estimate uses one bulk of two genes. The
  Wald and profile intervals are then one-observation approximations,
  whose calibration is what the coverage measures.
